# Ulcerative colitis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the intestine and appendix > Ulcerative colitis*

[Original Article Link](/library/eS0xA2)

---

## Summary

Ulcerative <u>colitis</u> is a type of <u>chronic inflammatory bowel disease</u> (<u>IBD</u>) characterized by <u>mucosal</u> inflammation of the <u>colon</u> that typically starts in the <u>rectum</u> and may extend proximally affecting the <u>distal</u> <u>colon</u> or the entire <u>colon</u> up to the <u>cecum</u>. The most common clinical feature is bloody <u>diarrhea</u>, often accompanied by abdominal <u>pain</u>, <u>fecal urgency</u>, and <u>tenesmus</u>. Extraintestinal manifestations such as <u>arthritis</u>, <u>uveitis</u>, <u>erythema nodosum</u>, and <u>primary sclerosing cholangitis</u> can also occur. Diagnosis is confirmed by <u>ileocolonoscopy</u> with <u>biopsy</u>, while laboratory (e.g., <u>ESR</u>, <u>CRP</u>) and stool studies (e.g., <u>fecal calprotectin</u>) help assess disease severity. Treatment depends on disease severity, ranging from <u>5-ASA</u> preparations for mild disease to <u>systemic immunomodulatory medications</u> for severe disease. Major complications include <u>toxic megacolon</u>, perforation, and an increased risk of <u>colorectal cancer</u>, which necessitates regular endoscopic screening. A restorative <u>proctocolectomy</u> is a curative surgical option for patients with refractory disease or complications.




![Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis: Differences](media/small_5dfa161c8ed3c.jpg)

Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis: Differences

---

## Epidemiology

* <u>Prevalence</u> 

* Approx. 1.2 million adults in the US are affected by ulcerative <u>colitis</u>.[[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)

* Ethnicity

* Higher in White populations than in Black, Hispanic, or Asian populations

* Highest among individuals of <u>Ashkenazi Jewish descent</u>

* <u>Incidence</u>

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 20–30 years of age [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)

* Another smaller peak may be observed in individuals > 55 years of age. [[2]](/library/Rn0lGg)

* Childhood onset occurs in > 10% of patients; see “<u>IBD in children</u>.” [[3]](/library/gDdFdH0)

* ♂=♀ [[4]](/library/lbcvFa0)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

### <u>Risk factors</u> [[2]](/library/Rn0lGg)[[5]](/library/wLYh-p)[[6]](/library/TYa6oQ)




* Genetic predisposition (e.g., <u>HLA-B27</u> association)

* Ethnicity (White populations, individuals of <u>Ashkenazi Jewish descent</u>)

* <u>Family history</u> of <u>inflammatory bowel disease</u>

* History of intestinal infections

* Increased fat intake (especially saturated fat and animal fat)

* <u>Oral contraceptive</u> use

* <u>NSAIDs</u> may exacerbate ulcerative <u>colitis</u>.





### Protective factors [[5]](/library/wLYh-p)[[6]](/library/TYa6oQ)




* <u>Appendectomy</u>

* Smoking

---

## Pathophysiology

The exact mechanism is unknown but studies suggest that ulcerative <u>colitis</u> is caused by abnormal interactions between host <u>immune cells</u> and <u>commensal</u> bacteria. [[5]](/library/wLYh-p)[[6]](/library/TYa6oQ)




* Dysregulation of intestinal <u>epithelium</u>: increased permeability for luminal bacteria  → activation of <u>macrophages</u> and <u>dendritic cells</u> → <u>antigen</u> presentation to <u>macrophages</u> and naive <u>CD4+</u> cells leads to:

* Secretion of <u>proinflammatory cytokines</u> (<u>IL-6</u>, <u>IL-12</u>, <u>TNF-α</u>) and <u>chemokines</u> (CXCL1, CXCL3, and CXCL8) → recruitment of other <u>immune cells</u> (e.g., <u>neutrophils</u>) to the site

* Differentiation of naive <u>CD4+</u> cells to <u>Th2</u> effector cells

* Recruitment of <u>natural killer cells</u>

* Dysregulation of the <u>immune system</u>: upregulation of lymphatic cell activity (<u>T cells</u>, <u>B cells</u>, <u>plasma cells</u>) in bowel walls → enhanced immune reaction and cytotoxic effect on <u>colonic</u> <u>epithelium</u> → inflammation with local tissue damage (<u>ulcerations</u>, <u>erosions</u>, <u>necrosis</u>) in the <u>submucosa</u> and <u>mucosa</u>

* <u>Autoantibodies</u> (<u>pANCA</u>) against cells of the intestinal <u>epithelium</u>

* <u>Th2 cell</u>-mediated response

* Pattern of involvement

* Ascending inflammation that begins in the <u>rectum</u> and spreads continuously proximally throughout the <u>colon</u>

* Inflammation is limited to the <u>mucosa</u> and <u>submucosa</u>.





> [!NOTE]
> The <u>rectum</u> is always involved in ulcerative <u>colitis</u>.

---

## Clinical features

### Intestinal features




* Bloody <u>diarrhea</u> with mucus (<u>hematochezia</u>)

* <u>Fecal urgency</u>

* Increased stool frequency

* Abdominal <u>pain</u> and cramps

* <u>Tenesmus</u>





### Extraintestinal features of ulcerative colitis




* General: fatigue, <u>fever</u>

* Skeletal:  (most common extraintestinal feature of ulcerative <u>colitis</u>): <u>arthritis</u>, <u>ankylosing spondylitis</u>, <u>sacroiliitis</u> [[9]](/library/SoYyYJ)[[10]](/library/hoYcbJ)

* Ocular: <u>uveitis</u>, <u>episcleritis</u>, <u>iritis</u>

* Biliary: <u>primary sclerosing cholangitis</u> (it is rare for patients with ulcerative <u>colitis</u> to develop <u>PSC</u>, but up to 90% of all patients with <u>PSC</u> will also have ulcerative <u>colitis</u>)

* Cutaneous

* <u>Erythema nodosum</u>

* <u>Pyoderma gangrenosum</u>

* <u>Aphthous stomatitis</u>

* Pyostomatitis vegetans

* A very rare condition that is associated with other cutaneous diseases and <u>inflammatory bowel disease</u>, particularly ulcerative <u>colitis</u>

* Manifests with multiple aphthae and <u>pustules</u> of the oral <u>mucosa</u>





> [!NOTE]
> <u>PSC</u> is often associated with <u>inflammatory bowel disease</u>, especially ulcerative <u>colitis</u>. However, only approximately 4% of patients with <u>inflammatory bowel disease</u> develop <u>PSC</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> “ULCCCERS:” Ulcers, Large intestine, Continuous/Colon cancer/Crypt <u>abscesses</u>, Extends proximally, Red <u>diarrhea</u>, and Sclerosing <u>cholangitis</u> are the characteristics of ulcerative <u>colitis</u>.




![Extraintestinal manifestations of inflammatory bowel disease](media/nbq0tsfqncfr7jzf9dzx6mgn.jpg)

Extraintestinal manifestations of inflammatory bowel disease




### Disease course




* Chronic intermittent

* Most common course

* Exacerbation is followed by complete remission.

* Chronic continuous

* Complete remission does not occur.

* Disease severity varies.

* Acute fulminant (i.e., <u>acute severe ulcerative colitis</u>)

* Sudden onset

* Severe <u>diarrhea</u>, <u>dehydration</u>, <u>shock</u>

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)




The diagnosis is based on clinical features, endoscopic and pathology findings. [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)




* Suspect ulcerative <u>colitis</u> in patients with <u>hematochezia</u>, increased stool frequency, and <u>fecal urgency</u>.

* Assess for <u>extraintestinal features of ulcerative colitis</u>.

* Order <u>laboratory studies</u> to: 

* Rule out <u>infectious gastroenteritis</u>

* Assess disease severity (e.g., baseline levels of <u>CRP</u>, <u>fecal calprotectin</u>) [[11]](/library/6-djys0)

* Consult gastroenterology for an <u>ileocolonoscopy</u> with <u>biopsy</u> to:

* Confirm the <u>diagnosis of ulcerative colitis</u>

* Determine the <u>extent of disease in ulcerative colitis</u> and <u>severity of ulcerative colitis</u>

* Assess disease severity

* See "<u>Classification of ulcerative colitis by severity</u>."

* Identify patients with <u>acute severe ulcerative colitis</u> (<u>ASUC</u>).

* Consider CT or <u>MRI</u> abdomen if endoscopy is contraindicated.





### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)




Stool testing for <u>infectious gastroenteritis</u> is indicated in all patients. Blood tests are not required for diagnosis, but help assess disease activity and severity.




* Blood tests

* <u>CBC</u>: <u>anemia</u>, <u>leukocytosis</u>, <u>thrombocytosis</u> [[4]](/library/lbcvFa0)

* <u>ESR</u>, <u>CRP</u>: Elevated levels may indicate active ulcerative <u>colitis</u> and often correlate with disease severity.

* <u>Hypoalbuminemia</u>: associated with a poor prognosis and more severe disease

* <u>ALP</u>, <u>GGT</u>: elevated in patients with concurrent <u>PSC</u>

* <u>pANCA</u>

* Not recommended to establish diagnosis, monitor disease activity, or determine prognosis [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)

* Elevated in up to 70% of patients with ulcerative <u>colitis</u>  [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)

* <u>Stool diagnostic studies</u> [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)[[11]](/library/6-djys0)

* <u>Stool test for Clostridioides difficile infection</u>   [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)[[11]](/library/6-djys0)

* <u>Fecal calprotectin</u>: to monitor disease activity and response to therapy  [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)[[11]](/library/6-djys0)

* <u>GI PCR panel</u>: Consider based on clinical features and <u>risk factors for diarrhea</u>. [[11]](/library/6-djys0)

* <u>Stool culture</u> and microscopy: to assess for bacteria, <u>ova</u>, and <u>parasites</u> if a <u>GI PCR panel</u> is not available





> [!TIP]
> <u>CRP</u>, <u>ESR</u>, or <u>hemoglobin</u> levels are not required for the <u>diagnosis of ulcerative colitis</u>; they help determine disease severity.




> [!TIP]
> <u>Hypoalbuminemia</u> and ↑ <u>CRP</u> are significant poor prognostic factors. Other factors include age < 40 years at diagnosis, extensive ulcerative <u>colitis</u>, and severe disease on endoscopic evaluation scores. [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)




### Endoscopy [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)



* <u>Ileocolonoscopy</u>

* Recommended method for diagnosis and disease monitoring [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)

* Severe disease is a <u>relative contraindication</u>.  [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)

* See "<u>Histopathology</u> findings" in "Pathology".




| Endoscopic findings in ulcerative colitis |  |
| --- | --- |
| Early stages | Chronic disease |
| <br><br>* Inflamed, <u>erythematous</u>, <u>edematous</u> <u>mucosa</u><br><br>* <u>Friable</u> <u>mucosa</u> with bleeding on contact with endoscope<br><br>* <u>Fibrin</u>-covered <u>ulcers</u><br><br>* Small <u>mucosal</u> <u>ulcerations</u><br><br>* Loss of <u>superficial</u> vascular pattern<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Loss of <u>mucosal</u> folds<br><br>* Loss of <u>haustra</u><br><br>* Strictures<br><br>* Deep <u>ulcerations</u><br><br>* Pseudopolyps <br><br>* Raised areas of normal <u>mucosal</u> tissue that result from repeated cycles of <u>ulceration</u> and healing<br><br>* <u>Ulceration</u> → formation of granulation tissue → deposition of granulation tissue → epithelialization<br><br>* Morphologically resemble polyps but do not undergo <u>neoplastic</u> transformation<br><br>* Found in advanced disease<br><br><br> |





* <u>Sigmoidoscopy</u> [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)

* Indications

* Initially used as an alternative to <u>ileocolonoscopy</u>, e.g., in <u>ASUC</u>

* Monitoring treatment response

* Findings are similar to <u>ileocolonoscopy</u> findings.

* <u>EGD</u>: recommended for patients with upper GI symptoms to rule out <u>Crohn disease</u>  [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)





> [!WARNING]
> There is a high risk for <u>colonic</u> perforation in severe ulcerative <u>colitis</u>; caution should be used when performing <u>biopsies</u>.

### Imaging studies [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)




* Not routinely recommended for diagnosis

* Adjunct to endoscopy, particularly for the detection of complications; , or if endoscopy is not possible. [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)





#### <u>Abdominal x-rays</u> [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)




* Indication: initial and serial evaluation of suspected <u>ASUC</u>

* Findings

* Typically normal in mild-to-moderate disease

* Severe disease

* Loss of <u>colonic haustra</u> (lead pipe appearance)

* Increased bowel wall thickness

* May show signs of complications, e.g.:

* <u>Toxic megacolon</u>: massive distention

* <u>Ulceration</u>: segmental dilation with irregular edges outlined by gas [[12]](/library/sxctBe0)

* Perforation: <u>pneumoperitoneum</u>   [[13]](/library/wichFX0)





![Lead pipe sign](media/rnjph7sk8egkcn7ndrmdl4oy.jpg)

Lead pipe sign

![Pneumoperitoneum and Pneumoretroperitoneum](media/stawo7szi6u9gooseymrjilo.jpg)

Pneumoperitoneum and Pneumoretroperitoneum




#### CT or <u>MRI</u> abdomen [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)[[13]](/library/wichFX0)




* Indications

* Abdominal symptoms unexplained by endoscopic findings [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)

* Evaluation of <u>proximal</u> disease involvement when endoscopy is not feasible

* Suspected complications (e.g., <u>bowel perforation</u>)

* Differentiation from other conditions, e.g., <u>Crohn disease</u> [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)

* Findings

* Loss of <u>haustra</u>

* Increased bowel wall thickness

* Mural hyperenhancement

* Signs of complications (similar to <u>abdominal x-ray</u> findings)





#### <u>Barium enema</u> <u>radiography</u> [[12]](/library/sxctBe0)




The role of <u>barium enema</u> is limited, as it is less sensitive than other imaging modalities and is contraindicated in patients with active disease.




* Indication: <u>Colonoscopy</u> is contraindicated and other <u>cross-sectional imaging</u> (e.g., CT, <u>MRI</u>) is not available.

* Findings

* Granular appearance of the <u>mucosa</u>

* Deep <u>ulcerations</u>

* Loss of <u>haustra</u>

* <u>Pseudopolyps</u> that appear as filling defects





#### Abdominal <u>ultrasound</u>  [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)




* Indication: monitoring disease activity and treatment response

* Findings: increased bowel wall thickness

## Pathology

### Gross pathology




See “<u>Endoscopic findings in ulcerative colitis</u>” in “Diagnostics.”




### <u>Histopathology</u> findings




* Early stages

* <u>Granulocyte</u> (<u>neutrophil</u>) infiltration: limited to <u>mucosa</u> and <u>submucosa</u>

* Crypt abscesses: an infiltration of <u>neutrophils</u> into the lumen of <u>intestinal crypts</u> due to a breakdown of the crypt <u>epithelium</u>

* Chronic disease

* <u>Lymphocyte</u> infiltration

* <u>Mucosal</u> <u>atrophy</u>

* Altered crypt architecture

* Branching of crypts

* Irregularities in size and shape

* <u>Epithelial</u> <u>dysplasia</u>





> [!NOTE]
> In ulcerative <u>colitis</u>, the extent of intestinal inflammation is limited to the <u>mucosa</u> and <u>submucosa</u>. In contrast, <u>Crohn disease</u> shows a <u>transmural</u> pattern of intestinal involvement.




> [!NOTE]
> <u>Noncaseating granulomas</u> are seen in <u>Crohn disease</u> but are not a feature of ulcerative <u>colitis</u>!

## Management

### General principles [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)




The goal of treatment is clinical and endoscopic remission.




* Consult gastroenterology before starting management.

* Provide <u>supportive care</u> measures for all patients.

* Choice of pharmacological therapy is based on the <u>classification of ulcerative colitis by severity</u> and patient-specific prognostic factors.

* Surgical management should be considered if medical therapy is unsuccessful or complications occur.

* Long-term management includes:

* Monitoring for complications related to the disease and its treatment.

* <u>Screening for colorectal cancer</u> and other common comorbidities (e.g., <u>depression</u> and <u>anxiety</u>).





> [!TIP]
> While most cases of ulcerative <u>colitis</u> can be managed in an outpatient setting, patients with <u>ASUC</u> should be admitted for management.




### <u>Supportive care</u> [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)




* <u>Pain management</u>

* Nonpharmacological measures, e.g., heating pads

* Consider <u>acetaminophen</u>, <u>anxiolytics</u>, and sedatives.

* Avoid <u>opioids</u> and <u>NSAIDs</u>.

* <u>Nutritional support</u>

* Assess for and manage <u>malnutrition</u>.

* Avoid <u>parenteral nutrition</u> unless required to improve <u>nutritional status</u> prior to <u>colectomy</u>.

* Probiotics: There is insufficient evidence to support their use.





### Surgical management [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)




Surgical treatment is curative for ulcerative <u>colitis</u> and reduces the risk of <u>colorectal cancer</u>. [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)




* Indications

* Complications of <u>ASUC</u>

* <u>Toxic megacolon</u>

* <u>Bowel perforation</u>

* Severe <u>hematochezia</u>

* <u>Multiorgan failure</u>

* Refractory ulcerative <u>colitis</u>;  (i.e., no response after 3–5 days of medical management and/or <u>glucocorticoid</u> dependence) [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)

* <u>Dysplasia</u> or <u>carcinoma</u>

* Procedure: restorative <u>proctocolectomy</u> with an ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (J pouch) 

* Resection of the entire <u>colon</u> and rectal <u>mucosa</u> while sparing the anal sphincters.

* Loops of <u>small intestine</u> (serving as the pouch) are used to create an artificial <u>rectum</u>, resulting in a continence-conserving connection between the <u>ileum</u> and <u>anus</u>.

* Complications of <u>surgery</u>

* Early (≤ 30 days): <u>anastomotic leak</u>, <u>pelvic</u> <u>sepsis</u>

* Late: bowel stricture, <u>bowel obstruction</u>, <u>fertility</u> issues, <u>sexual dysfunction</u> [[4]](/library/lbcvFa0)

* Most common late postoperative issue: <u>pouchitis</u> (increased stool frequency, <u>malaise</u>, and possibly incontinence caused by bacterial overgrowth)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Nutritional status</u> should be optimized before <u>colectomy</u> to improve patient outcomes.




![Restorative proctocolectomy](media/qwuwb2tet5u0sxe324i4f116.jpg)

Restorative proctocolectomy




### Long-term management of ulcerative colitis




* Disease monitoring

* <u>Flexible sigmoidoscopy</u>: 3–6 months after starting a new treatment [[4]](/library/lbcvFa0)

* Clinical assessment: every 3 months until remission, then every 6–12 months [[4]](/library/lbcvFa0)

* Follow-up after symptomatic remission

* Symptom assessment

* Inflammation biomarkers (i.e., <u>fecal calprotectin</u>, <u>fecal lactoferrin</u>, and/or serum <u>CRP</u>)  [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)[[11]](/library/6-djys0)

* <u>Colorectal cancer screening</u> [[14]](/library/4oY3XJ)[[15]](/library/a21QTT0)

* Start screening 8–10 years after the initial diagnosis or at the time of diagnosis of <u>primary sclerosing cholangitis</u>.

* Modality: <u>ileocolonoscopy</u> with <u>biopsies</u>

* Interval: every 1–5 years

* Additional measures [[16]](/library/hDdcVH0)[[17]](/library/J-dsys0)

* Annual <u>LFTs</u> to monitor for <u>primary sclerosing cholangitis</u> [[16]](/library/hDdcVH0)[[18]](/library/cydaVs0)

* See also “<u>Preventive care in IBD</u>.”

---

## Pharmacological therapy for ulcerative colitis

### General principles [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)



* The goal of pharmacological therapy is to induce and maintain disease remission. 

* <u>5-ASA</u> monotherapy are first-line in mild-to-moderate ulcerative <u>colitis</u>.

* Oral <u>glucocorticoids</u> are indicated for induction of remission of ulcerative <u>colitis</u> resistant to <u>5-ASA</u> monotherapy.

* <u>Systemic immunomodulators</u> (e.g., anti-TNF agents) should be considered for: [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)[[19]](/library/p-dLys0)

* Patients with moderate-to-severe ulcerative <u>colitis</u>

* Patients with poor prognosis factors:

* Age < 40 years at diagnosis

* ↑ <u>CRP</u>, <u>hypoalbuminemia</u>

* Extensive <u>colitis</u>, severe disease on endoscopy

* Hospitalization for <u>colitis</u>




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Glucocorticoids</u> should only be used for induction of remission and then gradually tapered. <u>Glucocorticoid-sparing agents</u> are preferred for <u>maintenance of remission</u>. [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)




### Induction of remission [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)

| --- | --- | --- |
| <br>Disease severity <br> |  | Agents |
| <br>Mild-to-moderate  [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)<br> |  | <br><br>* Ulcerative <u>proctitis</u><br><br>* First line: rectal <u>5-ASA</u> (e.g., <u>mesalamine</u> suppository DOSAGE OR <u>mesalamine</u> enema DOSAGE)  [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)<br><br>* Alternatives: rectal <u>glucocorticoids</u> (e.g., <u>budesonide</u> DOSAGE, <u>beclomethasone</u>), <u>tacrolimus</u> suppository, oral <u>budesonide</u> MMX® DOSAGE<br><br>* Left-sided or extensive <u>colitis</u><br><br>* First line: oral <u>5-ASA</u> DOSAGE PLUS rectal <u>5-ASA</u> (e.g., <u>mesalamine</u> enema DOSAGE)<br><br>* Alternative: oral <u>budesonide</u> MMX® DOSAGE  or rectal <u>glucocorticoids</u><br><br>* <u>5-ASA</u> nonresponders: oral <u>systemic glucocorticoids</u> (e.g., <u>prednisone</u> DOSAGE)<br><br><br> |
| <br>Moderate-to-severe  [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)<br> |  | <br><br>* Oral <u>glucocorticoids</u> (e.g., <u>budesonide</u> MMX® DOSAGE or <u>prednisone</u> DOSAGE)<br><br>* OR anti-TNF therapy (e.g., <u>infliximab</u>, <u>adalimumab</u>, <u>golimumab</u>) with a <u>thiopurine</u> (e.g., <u>azathioprine</u>)<br><br>* OR <u>JAK inhibitor</u> (e.g., <u>upadacitinib</u>)<br><br>* Other alternatives:  [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)<br><br>* <u>Integrin</u> <u>receptor</u> <u>antagonist</u> (e.g., <u>vedolizumab</u>)<br><br>* <u>IL-12</u>/23 inhibitor (e.g., <u>ustekinumab</u>)<br><br>* IL-23p19 inhibitor (e.g., <u>guselkumab</u>, <u>risankizumab</u>, <u>mirikizumab</u>)<br><br>* S1P <u>receptor</u> modulator (e.g., <u>ozanimod</u>, etrasimod)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Acute severe ulcerative colitis</u> |  | <br><br>* IV <u>glucocorticoids</u> (e.g., <u>methylprednisolone</u>  DOSAGE or <u>hydrocortisone</u> DOSAGE)<br><br>* <u>Cyclosporine</u> or <u>infliximab</u> if remission is not achieved after 3 days of IV <u>glucocorticoids</u>. [[1]](/library/1-d2ws0)<br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> For induction of remission, <u>azathioprine</u> may be considered in combination with anti-TNF agents, not as monotherapy.  [[14]](/library/4oY3XJ)




### <u>Maintenance of remission</u>




* The same agents used for induction should be continued for <u>maintenance of remission</u>, except for <u>glucocorticoids</u>.

* <u>Thiopurine</u> (e.g., <u>azathioprine</u>) monotherapy may be considered if remission was achieved with <u>glucocorticoids</u> alone.[[19]](/library/p-dLys0)





### Overview of <u>5-ASA</u> and <u>5-ASA derivatives</u> [[14]](/library/4oY3XJ)[[20]](/library/pbcLua0)




| <u>5-ASA</u> and 5-ASA derivatives |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Description | Mechanism of action | Adverse effects |
| Mesalamine | <br>* <u>5-ASA</u> alone (usually well-tolerated)<br><br> | <br><br>* The exact mechanism is unknown.<br><br>* Antiinflammatory, <u>immunosuppressive</u><br><br><br> | <br>* GI irritation: <u>nausea</u>, <u>diarrhea</u><br><br> |
| Olsalazine | <br>* Prodrug of <u>mesalamine</u><br><br> |  |  |
| Sulfasalazine | <br><br>* <u>5-ASA</u> bound to sulfapyridine as a carrier<br><br>* May be used in patients with ulcerative <u>colitis</u> with inflammatory <u>arthritis</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Metabolized to sulfapyridine and <u>mesalamine</u> by <u>colonic</u> bacteria<br><br>* Sulfapyridine: antibacterial; responsible for most of the adverse effects<br><br>* Sulfapyridine has proven to have beneficial effects in patients with rheumatic disease.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Headache</u>, fatigue, <u>malaise</u>, <u>depression</u><br><br>* <u>Megaloblastic anemia</u> and <u>folate deficiency</u> due to interference with <u>folate</u> metabolism  [[20]](/library/pbcLua0)<br><br>* <u>Immune thrombocytopenia</u> [[21]](/library/hbbctH)<br><br>* <u>Neutropenia</u> [[22]](/library/kXVmyG0)<br><br>* Transient <u>oligospermia</u><br><br>* Reactions to the sulfa moiety: <u>allergic reactions</u>, <u>sulfonamide</u> toxicity<br><br><br> |

## Complications

* ↑ Risk of cancer (see “<u>Long-term management of ulcerative colitis</u>” for screening protocol) 

* Risk increases with duration and/or extent of disease (e.g., pancolitis).

* <u>Colorectal carcinoma</u> risk is not significantly increased in patients with mild ulcerative <u>colitis</u>.

* <u>Toxic megacolon</u>

* Fulminant colitis: severe bowel inflammation that typically causes > 10 stools per day, <u>lower gastrointestinal bleeding</u>, abdominal <u>pain</u>, and abdominal distention

* <u>Gastrointestinal bleeding</u> (both acute and chronic)

* Perforation → <u>peritonitis</u> (see “<u>Gastrointestinal perforation</u>”)

* <u>Colonic stricture</u>

* <u>Amyloidosis</u>





References:[[23]](/library/a9aQN5)




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.

## Special patient groups

### Inflammatory bowel disease in children [[3]](/library/gDdFdH0)[[24]](/library/-BdDWs0)[[25]](/library/-DdDSH0)




#### <u>Epidemiology</u>




* The <u>incidence</u> of <u>IBD in children</u> is rising, especially very early onset <u>IBD</u> (before 6 years of age). [[3]](/library/gDdFdH0)[[26]](/library/SDdydH0)

* <u>Prevalence</u>: 77 per 100,000 [[3]](/library/gDdFdH0)





#### Clinical features [[3]](/library/gDdFdH0)[[25]](/library/-DdDSH0)




The <u>clinical features of IBD</u> are similar in adults and children. Additionally, in children, <u>IBD</u> is characterized by: [[3]](/library/gDdFdH0)




* <u>Delayed onset of puberty</u>

* <u>Growth stunting</u> (more commonly associated with <u>Crohn disease</u>) [[16]](/library/hDdcVH0)

* Increased risk of extraintestinal symptoms  [[24]](/library/-BdDWs0)[[25]](/library/-DdDSH0)

* Extraintestinal symptoms may precede gastrointestinal symptoms by months or years.

* Approx. 25% of children have extraintestinal symptoms at diagnosis. [[24]](/library/-BdDWs0)

* See “<u>Extraintestinal symptoms of Crohn disease</u>” and “<u>Extraintestinal symptoms of ulcerative colitis</u>.”

* Increased risk of severe disease and complications





#### Red flags for IBD in children [[3]](/library/gDdFdH0)




Any of the following features in a child with chronic (≥ 4 weeks) abdominal <u>pain</u> and/or <u>diarrhea</u> should prompt evaluation for <u>IBD</u>.




* Major red flags for IBD in children

* <u>Rectal bleeding</u>

* Perianal findings (e.g., <u>perianal fistula</u>, <u>perianal abscess</u>, perianal <u>ulcers</u>)

* Minor red flags for IBD in children

* <u>First-degree relative</u> with <u>IBD</u>

* Unplanned weight loss

* <u>Extraintestinal symptoms of ulcerative colitis</u> or <u>extraintestinal symptoms of Crohn disease</u>





#### Diagnosis of IBD in children [[3]](/library/gDdFdH0)[[24]](/library/-BdDWs0)[[25]](/library/-DdDSH0)[[27]](/library/N7b-NE)




* Assess for <u>red flags for IBD in children</u>.

* Obtain <u>CBC</u>, <u>inflammatory markers</u> (<u>CRP</u>, <u>ESR</u>), <u>liver chemistries</u>, and stool studies. [[28]](/library/CBdq1s0)

* Normal laboratory findings do not rule out <u>IBD</u>.

* See “<u>Laboratory studies</u>” in “<u>Diagnostics for ulcerative colitis</u>” or “<u>Diagnostics for Crohn disease</u>” for details.

* Refer for <u>ileocolonoscopy</u> and <u>EGD</u> as indicated. [[25]](/library/-DdDSH0)[[29]](/library/0ydeds0)

* <u>Major red flags for IBD in children</u>: Refer for endoscopy.

* <u>Minor red flags for IBD in children</u>: Consider a risk-<u>stratified</u> approach based on <u>fecal calprotectin</u> levels to determine the need for endoscopy. [[3]](/library/gDdFdH0)

* <u>Fecal calprotectin</u> > 250 mcg/g: Refer for endoscopy.

* <u>Fecal calprotectin</u> 50–250 mcg/g: Consider endoscopy based on <u>shared decision-making</u>.

* <u>Fecal calprotectin</u> < 50 mcg/g: <u>IBD</u> is excluded; consider other <u>causes of abdominal pain in children</u>.

* Imaging is indicated as an adjunctive diagnostic modality to determine the extent and severity of bowel involvement. [[24]](/library/-BdDWs0)[[25]](/library/-DdDSH0)[[29]](/library/0ydeds0)

* <u>Small bowel</u> imaging is recommended for all patients (unless endoscopic and <u>histology</u> findings are characteristic of ulcerative <u>colitis</u>). [[25]](/library/-DdDSH0)

* <u>MR enterography</u> is the preferred imaging modality. [[25]](/library/-DdDSH0)[[27]](/library/N7b-NE)[[30]](/library/J8dsn70)

* Wireless <u>capsule endoscopy</u> may be considered if conventional endoscopy or imaging is not feasible. [[25]](/library/-DdDSH0)[[30]](/library/J8dsn70)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Fecal calprotectin</u> < 50 mcg/g excludes <u>IBD</u>. [[3]](/library/gDdFdH0)




#### Management[[3]](/library/gDdFdH0)[[24]](/library/-BdDWs0)




Multidisciplinary management (including a pediatric gastroenterologist, nutritionist, primary care physician, and psychologist) is recommended. [[3]](/library/gDdFdH0)




* <u>Treatment of ulcerative colitis</u> is similar in children and adults, except <u>thiopurines</u> are not recommended for induction of remission in children. [[3]](/library/gDdFdH0)[[16]](/library/hDdcVH0)[[31]](/library/9wdNOH0)[[32]](/library/8wdOkH0)

* <u>Treatment of Crohn disease</u> is similar in children and adults, with the following exceptions for children: [[3]](/library/gDdFdH0)[[27]](/library/N7b-NE)

* Early initiation of anti-TNF therapy may be considered if prognostic indicators are poor.

* Exclusive <u>enteral nutrition</u> for 6–8 weeks (instead of <u>glucocorticoids</u>) may be considered to induce remission in selected patients.

* Long-term management of <u>IBD</u> is similar for children and adults.

* See “<u>Long-term management of ulcerative colitis</u>” and “<u>Long-term management of Crohn disease</u>” for details.

* In children, also monitor for <u>growth faltering</u> and <u>delayed onset of puberty</u>. [[16]](/library/hDdcVH0)

* See also “<u>Preventive care in IBD</u>” for details on <u>vaccination</u> and screening for other complications.





> [!WARNING]
> The transition from a pediatric to an adult care team must be well coordinated to avoid disease complications and/or relapse. [[3]](/library/gDdFdH0)




#### Inflammatory bowel disease in pregnancy [[33]](/library/3K1ST30)[[34]](/library/RK1lT30)




#### <u>Fertility</u> and <u>preconception counseling</u>




* <u>Fertility</u> is not affected in women with <u>IBD</u> in remission and no history of abdominal <u>surgery</u>.

* Women with active disease have decreased <u>fertility rates</u>.

* Pharmacological therapy for <u>IBD</u> does not impact <u>fertility</u>.

* Active disease at <u>conception</u> increases the risk of persistently active disease during <u>gestation</u>.

* Active disease is associated with an increased risk of <u>preterm birth</u> and <u>low birth weight</u>.

* Patients who wish to conceive should be on appropriate pharmacological therapy to maintain disease remission.

* With the exception of <u>methotrexate</u>, all other treatments can be continued at <u>conception</u>.





#### Disease management during <u>pregnancy</u>




* Most medications used in the treatment of <u>IBD</u> are considered safe during <u>pregnancy</u>.

* <u>Glucocorticoids</u>;  are indicated for disease flares but should be avoided as <u>maintenance therapy</u> because of the increased risk of <u>gestational diabetes</u>, <u>preterm birth</u>, and <u>low birth weight</u>.

* <u>5-ASA</u>, <u>5-ASA derivatives</u>, immunomodulators, and <u>biopharmaceuticals</u> can be used during <u>pregnancy</u>.

* Monotherapy is preferred for <u>maintenance treatment</u> to reduce the risk of adverse effects.
